extracted.intended_audience: NLP / ML researchers and practitioners studying large language model behavior, interpretability, and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for assessing LLM behavior across math reasoning, physical modelling, problem generation, explanations, and tool/environment interaction. Covers what makes solutions, explanations, and tool-mediated behaviors high- or low-quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate mathematical method selection and correct application
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an appropriate optimisation/analysis technique for the problem (e.g., Lagrange multipliers for minimizing x^2+y^2 subject to a constraint) and apply it correctly; incorrect application indicates lack of comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts two models: both 'realize that the method of Lagrange multipliers is useful', but ChatGPT 'applies this method in an incorrect way' while GPT-4 'produces a sound argument'. Use correct gradient/equation setup, include constraint function g(x,y), equate gradient components, and solve the resulting system; treat misapplication as a substantive error.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and justify modelling assumptions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When building a physical or applied model, list and justify simplifying assumptions (shape, homogeneity, initial conditions, ignored effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: iron-ball assumptions (spherical, homogeneous, density, melting point, starting orbit, ignoring gravity/drag/radiation losses) and egg example assumptions (bag width, bag thickness, tensile strength). Explicit assumptions help readers judge applicability and limitations of the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the relevant physical factors (weight, tensile strength, safety factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model real-world tasks by including the physically relevant quantities (e.g., weight and tensile strength vs. mere volume when estimating how many plastic bags are needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GPT-4's egg answer models mass from volume and gold density and estimates forces on a bag, then suggests applying a safety factor; ChatGPT's failure was focusing only on volume. Use density, forces (mg), material strength, geometry, and safety factors rather than irrelevant metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and model the governing physical processes (e.g., heat conductance, radiation, inverse-square law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and apply the correct physics (radiation intensity decay with distance, heat capacity, latent heat, conduction/convection/radiation losses) when the problem depends on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iron-ball example: use inverse-square law for solar intensity, cross-sectional area for absorbed power, specific heat and latent heat to compute temperature change, and integrate power over time/distance. Note which processes are neglected and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arithmetic and calculation errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric and algebraic mistakes are a common failure mode and can make otherwise-correct reasoning produce wrong final answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document observes that GPT-4's modelling may still contain calculation mistakes. Treat calculation errors as distinct from modelling errors and address them via verification, symbolic algebra, or external computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate calculation errors via external code execution
rubrics_metrics.description: When precise calculation is required, have the model produce code for an external executor to run, then incorporate the executed results back into reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example workflow: prompt the model to output a Python snippet that computes the numeric result (the paper shows an example wrapped with tags <b>...<e> and printing a LaTeX boxed answer). The external execution reduces human-model arithmetic mistakes; be explicit about input/output formatting when orchestrating code execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow prompt constraints when generating new problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to generate problem variants under specific constraints (e.g., content modification, difficulty enhancement, include a specific number), satisfy those constraints exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: content modification should keep structure but change names/values; difficulty enhancement should add steps/constraints; a request to 'add a sentence in the middle that includes the number 100' must be followed literally. Failure to obey prompt constraints is an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content modification should preserve structure but change surface details
rubrics_metrics.description: Create variants that maintain underlying logical structure and solution path while altering characters, objects, or numeric values to appear different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by transforming a beach/animal-cracker problem into a zoo/pretzel problem: same combinatorial logic but new surface context. This preserves pedagogical intent while producing a 'different-looking' problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty enhancement by adding steps, constraints, or complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a problem harder, add intermediate constraints, additional calculations, or mechanisms that increase multi-step reasoning rather than merely scaling numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: inserting a discount threshold ($100) before resale changes the optimization and introduces conditional reasoning; increasing complexity should require additional logical steps rather than trivial arithmetic scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation quality requires emulating the explaining agent (PE) and generative process (PG)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality explanations come from the model's ability to emulate both the persona/role of the explaining agent and the generative process that produced the output being explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper states: 'When the LLM can emulate the explaining agent PE and generative process PG well, the explanation is high quality and useful.' Use accurate modeling of the generator and plausible explaining persona to produce faithful, understandable explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match persona and audience when explaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an explanation style and level matching the intended audience (e.g., domain expert vs. a 4-year-old). Mismatched persona degrades usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asking the model to be both an astrophysicist and then suddenly a 4-year-old demonstrates that persona mismatch can produce unhelpful replies. Tailor vocabulary, depth, and analogies to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impose arbitrary output restrictions that make explanations useless
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid prompt-imposed constraints that eliminate necessary expressive capacity (e.g., forcing a one-word color response to complex questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure E.1's 'color robot' example shows that restricting responses to single color words yields nonsensical answers to non-color questions; such constraints produce poor explanations and should be avoided for explanation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulate the target model to explain its outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to explain another model's output, the explainer should emulate the target model's functional form and reasoning (e.g., linear regression coefficients) to provide correct, actionable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear-regression example: GPT-4 multiplies coefficient changes by feature changes and sums them to explain price change; successful emulation enables accurate interpretation of model behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool interaction: give one-action-at-a-time, step-by-step, actionable instructions and interpret results
rubrics_metrics.description: When instructing or interacting with a human or agent in an environment, issue single, clear actions sequentially, request or interpret feedback after each, and adapt based on observed outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual handyman example: the agent asks the human to check thermostat mode, then furnace presence, then ducts, interprets replies, suggests next diagnostic step, and proposes contingency actions (call professional, use space heater). This iterative loop (action → observe → interpret → next action) is required for robust tool-mediated assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and use required APIs/functions when automating tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Before automating interactions (e.g., calendar management), enumerate the API functions needed (addEvent, removeEvent, getEvents, updateEvent) and then use them in the dialogue to carry out user requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calendar example: the system lists functions, then demonstrates queries using getEvents and addEvent. Explicitly documenting available operations and their signatures improves safe, correct automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When executing environment/system commands, include plan, command, output interpretation, failure diagnosis, and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: For command-driven interactions, present a concise plan, run a command, parse its output, record whether it failed, and list possible reasons and alternative actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kali/hacking example demonstrates a structured loop: single-line reasoning, execute 'nmap', interpret results, note failure status, propose hypotheses for failure, then pick next command. Use the pattern: REASONING → COMMAND → OUTPUT → INTERPRETATION → DID IT FAIL? → POSSIBLE REASONS → NEXT ACTION.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow structured multi-step task guidelines in simulated file-system tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: When given a multi-step TODO with in-environment guidelines, follow the specified step order and produce both internal references and outward-facing artefacts per instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zoo 'emails' guideline: for each email, (1) read one email, (2) explore info and areas directories for relevant info via cd/dir, (3) draft an internal answer using echo referencing files as [ref: ...txt], (4) draft an external reply without references. Use documented file commands (type, cd, dir, echo, del, rename, move) to implement tasks and append replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to allowed command set in text-adventure environments
rubrics_metrics.description: In interactive fiction/TextWorld tasks, restrict actions to the provided command vocabulary (look, goal, inventory, go <dir>, examine, eat, open, close, drop, take, put, take from, insert, lock/unlock) and aim to accomplish the stated goal (e.g., ensure the Canadian chest is unlocked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TextWorld example lists explicit available commands and the game's goal. Use only those commands and the one-action-at-a-time pattern to explore rooms, inspect objects, open/close/lock/unlock containers, and progress toward the stated objective.
